rationale: C12 is a strong drafting-template candidate. Both are presidential letters addressing a Senate subcommittee's demand for Executive Branch information, affirming cooperation with Congress while invoking the public interest and constitutional separation of powers, citing a longstanding presidential practice of protecting confidential executive material, and directing executive officials not to disclose the requested information. The child generalizes C12's protection of confidential loyalty-investigation files into protection for candid internal Executive Branch advice. C22 and C19 contain related withholding machinery, but C12 supplies the closest combination of factual setting, constitutional rationale, historical precedent, and operative refusal.

shared_material.child_excerpt: every Executive Department or Agency must, upon the request of a Congressional Committee, expeditiously furnish information... However... the persons entrusted with power in any one of the three great branches of Government shall not encroach upon the authority confided to the others.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I wish to cooperate with your Subcommittee in every reasonable way... [but] Constitutional precedents... support without any question my authority to take the position I have in this matter.
shared_material.explanation: Both begin from a norm of congressional cooperation and then limit it by the President's constitutional responsibility for the Executive Branch.

shared_material.child_excerpt: throughout our history the President has withheld information whenever he found that what was sought was confidential or its disclosure would be incompatible with the public interest
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The authority of the President in this regard has been recognized since the beginnings of our Government... the Executive ought to communicate only such papers as the public good would permit, and ought to refuse those the disclosure of which would be contrary to the public interest.
shared_material.explanation: This is distinctive parallel language and reasoning about historical presidential authority to withhold confidential information when disclosure conflicts with the public interest.

shared_material.child_excerpt: you will instruct employees of your Department... not to testify to any such conversations or communications or to produce any such documents or reproductions.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I have felt obliged, therefore, to direct the Secretary of State, the Attorney General and the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission not to comply with your subpoenas.
shared_material.explanation: Both culminate in materially the same administrative mechanism: a presidential direction that named Executive Branch officials withhold specified information from a congressional subcommittee.

shared_material.child_excerpt: I direct this action so as to maintain the proper separation of powers between the Executive and Legislative Branches
shared_material.parent_excerpt: No President has ever complied with an order of the Legislative Branch directing the Executive Branch to produce confidential documents... [Presidents] have uniformly rejected such encroachments on the Constitutional power of the President.
shared_material.explanation: The child's express separation-of-powers justification closely adapts C12's constitutional anti-encroachment rationale.
